hero.name: Pallavi
hero.who: a 47-year-old bank cashier in Mysuru who feels tired and tense all day

story.b: Pallavi has worked at the cash counter of a bank branch in Mysuru for nineteen years. Lately she is tired by eleven in the morning, even after eight hours in bed. Her husband Suresh says she snores, and she often wakes with a dry mouth. At the counter, when the queue grows long before pension day, her shoulders creep up towards her ears and her breathing turns quick and shallow. She has never thought about her breathing. It just happens, like the ceiling fan turning. One evening her daughter Divya, home from college, watches her climb the stairs to their flat and asks why she is breathing through her mouth as if she has run a race.

ask.q: Pallavi is tired, snores and breathes fast under stress. What is a sensible first step?
o: Drink stronger coffee to get through the mornings
Ignore it, since breathing is automatic anyway
Start noticing how she breathes, and see a doctor about the snoring and tiredness
ask.why: Breathing happens on its own, but how we breathe can be noticed and gently changed. Strong coffee only covers the tiredness, and ignoring snoring can miss something worth checking. Paying attention and seeing a doctor gives Pallavi a safe, sensible place to start.

chapters.take: Something you do all day without thinking may be worth a closer look.

story.b: The doctor at a clinic near Kukkarahalli lake checks Pallavi and finds nothing serious. She suggests regular walks, better sleep habits and paying attention to how Pallavi breathes, and asks her to come back if the snoring gets worse. So Pallavi tries something simple on her evening walk to the vegetable stalls. She breathes only through her nose. It feels strange at first. On the slope near the main road, her mouth falls open without her noticing, and she has to slow down to keep it closed. After two weeks it is easier, and she reaches home calmer. At work she mentions it to her colleague Revathi. Revathi says people online tape their mouths shut at night.

ask.q: Revathi tells Pallavi to tape her mouth shut at night, as people do online. What should Pallavi do?
o: Keep practising nose breathing by day, and ask her doctor before trying any night-time method
Try it tonight, since it seems to work for people online
Give up on nose breathing, since nights are out of her control
ask.why: Daytime nose breathing is gentle and easy to practise. Night-time tricks from the internet may not suit everyone, especially with a blocked nose or other health issues, so checking with her doctor first is the safe move. Giving up throws away a habit that is slowly getting easier.

chapters.take: Try breathing through your nose. Ask a doctor before any night-time trick.

story.b: Pension day is the hardest day at Pallavi's counter. The queue stretches out of the door, the fan barely helps, and by noon her neck is stiff. This month she tries something between customers. While the note-counting machine whirs, she breathes in gently for a count of five and out for a count of five. Nobody notices. Just two or three slow breaths each time. Her shoulders drop a little. She does not feel transformed, but she feels less like a pressure cooker. Then, at half past twelve, a man at the front starts shouting that his pension has not been credited. He bangs his passbook on the counter, and Pallavi feels her breath jump into her throat.

ask.q: An angry customer is shouting, and Pallavi's breath turns quick and shallow. What could help in that moment?
o: Breathe faster to get more energy for the argument
Take a few slow, gentle breaths before she responds
Hold her breath and push through
ask.why: Quick, shallow breathing often goes with feeling tense, and holding the breath or speeding up may add to it. A few slow, gentle breaths are a simple way many people find calming. It will not fix the customer, but it may help Pallavi respond clearly instead of reacting.

chapters.take: When pressure rises, slow your breath. It can steady the rest of you.

story.b: Pallavi reads that many people may breathe more air than they need, and that some find breathing a little more lightly helps them feel calmer. She tries a soft version at night, lying in bed with the fan on low. After each easy exhale, she pauses for a few seconds before breathing in. No forcing, no counting to big numbers. If she feels any strain, she simply breathes normally. Some nights it helps her drift off. Some nights it makes no difference, and she lets it go. On Sunday her younger sister Latha visits with news. Latha, who has had asthma since childhood, found a video of a breath-holding challenge and wants to try it every morning.

ask.q: Latha, who has asthma, wants to try long breath-hold challenges from a video. What should Pallavi advise?
o: Hold as long as possible to build tolerance quickly
Copy the video exactly, since the instructor looks fit
Talk to her doctor first, and keep any practice gentle and short
ask.why: The idea of breathing more lightly is about gentle pauses, never straining. Long holds can be risky for some people, especially with asthma or heart conditions. Pushing for tolerance or copying a video ignores that. Checking with her doctor and staying gentle keeps Latha safe.

chapters.take: Gentle and light, never forced. Check with a doctor before stronger methods.

story.b: One lunch break, Pallavi looks at her tiffin. Soft idli, chutney and a banana. Yesterday it was upma, the day before, bread with jam. She cannot remember the last meal she really had to chew. She reads an idea that soft modern food gives our jaws far less work than they were built for, and that some researchers link this with narrower airways, though not everyone agrees. She cannot change her jaw at forty-seven, but chewing more seems a harmless thing to try. So she adds a few things. Carrot sticks, a handful of roasted chana, a proper chapati instead of bread. Her jaw feels tired the first week, which makes her laugh. Then Divya calls from her hostel, cheerfully listing noodle flavours.

ask.q: Divya lives on soft instant noodles and bread at her hostel. What small change could Pallavi suggest?
o: Add one food that needs real chewing, like carrots or roasted chana
Switch to liquid meals to save time
Chew gum all day instead of changing her food
ask.why: The idea is that soft diets give our jaws much less work than they were built for, though the science is still debated. Liquid meals mean even less chewing, and gum all day is no substitute for real food. Adding one firm, chewable food is a small, sensible change.

chapters.take: Give your jaw real work. Add one food that needs proper chewing.

story.b: Pallavi remembers her mother sitting on the verandah every morning before the milk came, eyes closed, gently closing one nostril and then the other. As a child she thought it was just an old habit. Now she joins a free morning yoga class in the park near her house, run by a retired teacher who has trained for many years. The teacher shows her five slow rounds of alternate nostril breathing, with long, easy exhales. No strain, no rushing. Pallavi tries it before bed and finds it a quiet way to end the day. When she tells Revathi, Revathi gets excited and shows her a reel of a very fast, forceful breathing method promising instant energy.

ask.q: Revathi wants to try an intense, rapid breathing method from a reel. What should Pallavi suggest?
o: Start with the most intense version for quick results
Begin with gentle practices from a trained teacher, and check with a doctor before intense methods
Skip breathing practices, since old methods have no value
ask.why: Gentle practices like alternate nostril breathing and long, slow exhales have been used for centuries and are easy to start. Intense methods are not right for everyone, so jumping in from a reel is risky. Dismissing old wisdom loses something useful. A trained teacher and a doctor's check keep it safe.

chapters.take: Old breathing practices can be a gift. Learn them gently, from someone trained.

story.b: Pallavi still works the same counter, and pension day is still pension day. But she walks to the market breathing through her nose without thinking about it. Between customers she takes two slow breaths, and her shoulders stay where they belong. Her tiffin has carrot sticks and chana, and Divya has started keeping peanuts in her hostel room. Most nights Pallavi does five rounds of alternate nostril breathing. At her follow-up visit, the doctor is pleased and tells her to carry on. Suresh says the snoring is quieter, though he admits he cannot be completely sure. Pallavi just smiles. The thing she did all day without thinking turned out to deserve a little thought.

chapters.take: Small, gentle changes to everyday breathing can make ordinary days feel calmer.
